title: Mary Latha Regini vs Maria James on 9 January, 2026

paragraphs.text:
C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 BEFORE THE MADURAI BENCH OF MADRAS HIGH COURT

 Reserved on : 05.11.2025

 Pronounced on : 09.01.2026

 CORAM:

 THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE P.VELMURUGAN

 and

 THE HONOURABLE MRS.JUSTICE L.VICTORIA GOWRI

 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021
 and
 CMP(MD)No.5884 of 2021

 Mary Latha Regini ... Appellant / Respondent


 Vs.

 Maria James ... Respondent / Petitioner



 PRAYER: Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed under Section 19(1) of the
 Family Court Act, 1984, to call for the records pertaining to the fair and
 decreetal order in I.D.O.P.No.86 of 2018 passed by the learned Family
 Court, Kannyakumari at Nagercoil dated 27.03.2019 and set aside the
 same.

 For Appellant : Mr.K.P.Narayana Kumar

 For Respondent : No appearance




 1/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 JUDGMENT

(Judgment of the Court was made by L.VICTORIA GOWRI, J.)


 This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed under Section 19 of the

 Family Courts Act, 1984, read with Section 55 of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869, to set aside the judgment and decree dated 27.03.2019 made in

 I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 on the file of the learned Family Court,

 Kanyakumari at Nagercoil, whereby the marriage between the appellant

 and the respondent solemnised on 08.05.2003 was dissolved under

 Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, on the ground of

 cruelty.
Prologue:

2. This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the

 judgment and decree of the learned Judge, Family Court, Kanyakumari

 at Nagercoil, in I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018, by which the respondent–

 husband’s petition under Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869, for dissolution of marriage on the ground of cruelty, came to be

 allowed and the marital tie between the parties was severed. The wife,

 who was the respondent before the learned Family Court, is the

 appellant before this Court.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

3. The appeal raises, in essence, the recurring question as to

 when a spouse’s protest, suspicion and complaint regarding the

 conduct and association of the other spouse crosses the line and

 becomes “cruelty” in law, and equally, whether such protest, if founded

 upon some admitted factual substratum, can at all be branded as

 reckless and unfounded so as to furnish a ground for divorce.
Case of the Husband before the learned Family Court:

4. The respondent-husband laid I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 under

 Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, seeking dissolution of

 his marriage with the appellant on the ground of cruelty and desertion.

 It is his case that the marriage between the parties was solemnised on

 08.05.2003 at the Church of Our Lady of Lourdes, Punnai Nagar,

 Nagercoil, according to Christian rites and customs and was duly

 registered under the Christian Marriage Act . Out of the wedlock, two

 male children, namely, Thinal (born on 24.02.2004) and Jasmine Girio

 (born on 26.09.2005) were born. Both spouses are educated and

 employed as teachers; the husband as a Selection Grade Teacher at

 Pallam and the wife as Headmistress of St. James High School,

 Vaniyakudi.

3/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

5. According to the husband, though the marriage subsisted in

 form, the appellant-wife never showed compassion, understanding, true

 love or affection. It is alleged that she persistently humiliated him, both

 at home and in public, including in the presence of neighbours,

 strangers and colleagues, by levelling wild accusations of adultery, and

 sodomy with young children, without any foundation. The husband

 would allege that these accusations were figments of imagination, for

 which she refused to correct herself despite his exhortations.

6. The husband further alleged that after the appellant took

 employment at Vaniyakudi, she gradually withdrew from the

 matrimonial home and ultimately left in the year 2004 along with her

 personal belongings and the minor children, ceased to discharge marital

 obligations, never cooked or cared for him, and refused to return to the

 matrimonial home, thereby causing mental cruelty and desertion. On

 these allegations, the husband approached the learned Family Court

 seeking dissolution of the marriage on the twin grounds of cruelty and

 desertion.

4/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 Case of the Wife before the learned Family Court:

7. The appellant-wife entered contest and filed a detailed counter,

 stoutly denying the allegations and, in turn, levelling specific allegations

 of dowry demand, financial exploitation, physical cruelty and immoral

 conduct on the part of the husband. The appellant would state that at

 the time of marriage, her parents gave 65 sovereigns of gold jewellery to

 her, Rs.3,00,000/- in cash and household articles worth Rs.1,00,000/-,

 apart from a gold chain of 7½ sovereigns to the husband. She lived with

 the husband at Pallam from 2003 to 2006 and commuted daily to

 Vaniyakudi for her work.

8. It is her case that, in 2004, the husband took away 45

 sovereigns of her gold jewellery and pledged the same in the bank to

 discharge his earlier debts; that he continuously harassed her

 demanding additional dowry and even pledged her thali chain in 2005.

 That on 21.08.2004 he assaulted her and drove her out of the

 matrimonial home to extract more money from her parental family, and

 that she was brought back on 26.12.2004 on his assurance of good

 behaviour.

5/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

9. She further alleged that, on the husband threatening to commit

 suicide, she was constrained to borrow Rs.1,50,000/- at 36% interest

 from her colleagues, namely, Dioceis Mary, Seeli and Amalapushpam,

 and handed it over to him to clear his debts. On the demise of her sister

 Jasmine on 16.05.2006, she shifted to her parental house at

 Vaniyakudi along with her mother and, at that time, the husband also

 lived with her there. It is alleged that during this period, he sold his

 Pallam house for Rs.2,00,000/- without her knowledge and, when

 questioned, took away the minor children and disappeared, compelling

 her to approach the police for their return.

10. The appellant further stated that, anticipating that she would

 get regular Government salary, the husband once again sought reunion

 and they stayed in a rented house at N.G.O. Colony in 2008, and later

 returned to Vaniyakudi. She claims to have spent about Rs.2,00,000/-

 from her arrears towards clearing his debts. At his instance, she also

 obtained a loan of Rs.3,00,000/- from the Teachers’ Society, out of

 which, according to her, the husband took Rs.2,70,000/- and

 absconded, leaving her to shoulder the repayment alone.




 6/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

11. The gravest allegation made by the wife is that the husband

 developed an undesirable association with a young man by name Ajith,

 hailing from Kootumangalam; that he used to visit a house at

 Kootumangalam frequently in 2014, return home late in the night, and

 later, in 2015, took a separate rented house at Pallam and stayed with

 the said Ajith, even admitting him in a local school showing himself as

 guardian. In this context, she claims to have lodged a complaint before

 the All Women Police Station, Colachel, wherein, according to her, the

 husband admitted that he stayed with a boy at Pallam.

12. The appellant would say that she placed her grievance before

 the Kootumangalam Village President and village elders; that the village

 President warned the husband and Ajith’s family; and that, in spite of

 such intervention, the husband continued his association with Ajith,

 thereby giving rise to her suspicion. She denies having deserted the

 husband, denies having humiliated him without basis and asserts that

 whatever she said and did was in response to his own conduct and

 financial and emotional abuse. She, therefore, prayed for dismissal of

 the divorce petition.

7/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 Proceedings before the learned Family Court:

13. Before the learned Family Court, the husband examined

 himself as P.W.1 and produced Exs.P1 to P5. The wife examined herself

 as R.W.1 and produced Exs.R1 to R4. The learned Family Court framed

 issues, inter alia, as to (i) whether the husband had proved cruelty, (ii)

 whether he had proved desertion, and (iii) whether he was entitled to a

 decree of divorce and consequential reliefs.

14. Ultimately, while holding that desertion was not proved, the

 learned Family Court concluded that the wife’s allegations about the

 husband’s association with Ajith and her imputations of

 immoral/unnatural conduct, being unsubstantiated and reckless,

 amounted to mental cruelty. On that basis alone, it granted a decree for

 dissolution of marriage, while also granting custody of the children to

 the wife and directing payment of monthly maintenance to them.
Grounds of Appeal:

15. Aggrieved, the wife has preferred the present appeal, raising

 the following, among other, grounds:

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 The order passed by the Family Court, Kanyakumari, on

 assumptions is unknown to law and liable to be interfered with. The

 learned Trial Court failed to see that the petitioner–husband, who

 approached the Court, had the burden to prove the allegations, and

 that the burden is not on the respondent–wife. The learned Trial Court

 ought to have dismissed the petition for dissolution of marriage, as the

 same was filed by the husband to shield his own illegality and

 misconduct. A person who has committed a wrong cannot be permitted

 to benefit from his own wrong. The factum of cruelty has to be decided

 on the circumstances of each case independently and on the totality of

 evidence. The specific allegation that the husband had a relationship

 with one Ajith has, according to the appellant, been substantially

 admitted by him in his deposition. The husband’s own testimony

 reveals an unexplained and unusual attachment with Ajith and his stay

 with the said boy, which the appellant was entitled to question; her

 reaction to that cannot be termed cruelty. A spouse’s protest against the

 illegal or unnatural behaviour of the other spouse cannot be termed

 cruelty; in other words, reality cannot be branded as cruelty. The

 discussion of the learned Trial Court is self-contradictory inasmuch as,

 in paragraphs 20 and 21 of the impugned judgment, it treats the

 disputes as trivial, yet in paragraphs 27 and 28 of the impugned

 judgment, it proceeds on assumptions to hold cruelty proved. The


 9/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 learned Trial Court failed to give due weight to the admitted fact of the

 husband’s stay with Ajith, thereby erroneously treating the appellant’s

 apprehensions as reckless.

16. Heard the learned counsel for the appeallant and carefully

 perused the materials available on record.
Points for Determination:

17. In the light of the pleadings, evidence and grounds of appeal,

 the following points arise for consideration:

(i) Whether the learned Family Court was right in holding that the

 respondent-husband had proved cruelty on the part of the appellant-

wife within the meaning of Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869?

(ii) Whether the decree of divorce granted by the learned Family

 Court is sustainable in law on the evidence on record?

(iii) What order is required to be made regarding the welfare of the

 minor children and maintenance, consequent upon the decision on

 Points (i) and (ii)?

10/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 Analysis:

18. It is well settled that while an Appellate Court would

 ordinarily be slow to interfere with findings of fact rendered by a Court

 of first instance, where such findings are based on misapplication of

 law, non-consideration of relevant evidence, or on impermissible

 assumptions, the Appellate Court is not only empowered but duty

 bound to reappreciate the evidence, particularly in matrimonial causes

 where the consequence is civil death of the marriage and serious social

 and personal repercussions.

19. The learned Family Court has extracted and relied on the

 principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Shobha Rani v.

 Madhukar Reddi1 , V. Bhagat v. D. Bhagat2 , Praveen Mehta v.

 Inderjit Mehta3 , Jayachandra v. Aneel Kaur4 , and Naveen Kohli v.

 Neelu Kohli5 , as also Sirajmohmedkhan Janmohamadkhan v.


 1 (1988) 1 SCC 105


 2 (1994) 1 SCC 337


 3 (2002) 5 SCC 706


 4 (2005) 2 SCC 22


 5 (2006) 4 SCC 558

 11/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 Hafizunnisa Yasinkhan6.

20. There can be no quarrel with the propositions emerging

 therefrom, namely, cruelty may be physical or mental, intentional or

 unintentional. Mental cruelty is a matter of inference from cumulative

 facts and circumstances and is to be assessed in the context of the

 parties’ social status, background and milieu. Mere trivial irritations,

 quarrels and normal “wear and tear” of married life do not amount to

 cruelty. Reckless, baseless and unsubstantiated allegations which

 gravely assault the character, honour and reputation of the other

 spouse can, in an appropriate case, constitute mental cruelty. The real

 question, however, is whether, on the facts of the present case, the

 appellant’s conduct answers the test of mental cruelty as understood in

 the above decisions. It is in this area that the learned Family Court, in

 the considered opinion of this Court, has misdirected itself.

21. The pivot of the learned Family Court’s finding on cruelty is

 that the wife allegedly levelled baseless imputations of

 immoral/unnatural conduct and undesirable association with the

 young man Ajith and, without any foundational material, branded the

 6 AIR 1981 SC 1972

 12/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 husband as one having sexual relations with young boys. Proceeding on

 that premise, the learned Family Court held that such aspersions

 constituted grave mental cruelty.

22. However, a careful reading of the cross-examination of R.W.1

 (wife) and P.W.1 (husband), which has been extracted in the lower Court

 judgment, presents a more nuanced picture. R.W.1, in her cross-

 examination, has consistently deposed that the husband and the boy

 Ajith used to go together wherever they went. The husband used to visit

 a certain house at Kootumangalam frequently and return late in the

 night. The husband admitted the said Ajith in a school at Pallam as the

 guardian of that boy. She approached the village elders and the Village

 President, and the President warned the husband and Ajith’s family.

 She had been raising these issues not only at home, but also before the

 schools where they worked and before the police, from 2015 onwards.

23. Significantly, the husband, in his cross-examination, has not

 denied that he had admitted Ajith in school as guardian, nor has he

 given any convincing explanation for his staying with and frequent

 association with the said boy. The learned Family Court has recorded



 13/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 that none from Ajith’s family has complained and, therefore, the wife’s

 allegations are reckless. This reasoning, with respect, reverses the

 burden and overlooks the admitted factual substratum.

24. It is not the appellant-wife who was living with Ajith; it was

 the husband who, by his own conduct in taking a separate rented

 house, staying with the boy and functioning as his guardian, created

 circumstances which, in a conservative and closely-knit rural milieu,

 would naturally generate suspicion. Once these admitted facts stand,

 the wife’s act of questioning such association and voicing her

 apprehensions cannot be branded as entirely baseless or malicious.

25. The law on cruelty does not intend to punish a spouse merely

 for reacting to unusual or unexplained conduct of the other spouse.

 When one spouse places herself in circumstances that objectively

 provoke anxiety, suspicion and protest, the other spouse’s reaction

 cannot, without more, be converted into a matrimonial offence. As the

 learned counsel for the appellant rightly contended, “reality cannot be

 cruelty”; a protest grounded in a real, admitted or reasonably

 perceivable situation cannot be equated with reckless slander.



 14/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

26. The learned Family Court has, in paragraphs 20 and 21 of its

 judgment, itself recorded that the parties had trivial disputes and

 misunderstandings. They had periods of reunion after temporary

 separation. There is a general breakdown in marital relations, with both

 sides having grievances. At the same time, in paragraphs 27 and 28 of

 the judgment, the learned Family Court proceeds to hold that the wife’s

 allegations, being reckless, by themselves constitute cruelty. This

 internal inconsistency, pointed out in the grounds of appeal, is well-

 founded. The learned Family Court has not undertaken the required

 exercise of assessing whether, in the context of the admitted facts, the

 wife’s statements were wholly unanchored or whether they were a

 response, albeit emotionally charged and perhaps exaggerated, to the

 husband’s own inexplicable proximity to Ajith.

27. Further, the learned Family Court has not adverted to the

 settled principle that to constitute cruelty, the conduct must be “grave

 and weighty” and of such severity as to make it impossible for the

 wronged spouse to reasonably be expected to live with the other. The

 evidence on record, even if accepted at the highest for the husband,

 only shows that the wife repeatedly complained, questioned and

 protested, sometimes in public fora. Annoyance, embarrassment or


 15/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 wounded ego cannot, by themselves, be equated with cruelty within the

 meaning of Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869.

28. The husband has not produced any independent witness from

 his workplace or from the village community to show that the wife

 indulged in a sustained campaign to defame him, or that his mental

 balance and social standing were so impaired by her conduct that

 cohabitation became impossible. His case rests substantially on his own

 testimony; there is no contemporaneous material (such as complaints

 by him, counselling records reflecting her refusal to mend her ways,

 etc.) to support the plea that she crossed the legal threshold of cruelty.

29. On the contrary, the wife’s version of dowry-related

 harassment, financial exploitation and domestic violence finds partial

 support in the admitted facts that the husband admits to sale of the

 Pallam house and to having remained away with the children,

 compelling her to go to the police (Ex.R1). He does not specifically deny

 having taken monies from the wife or having pressurised her to obtain

 loans, though the quantum and details are not fully proved.




 16/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

30. In a situation where both sides level allegations and the

 evidence is a word-against-word contest, Courts must tread cautiously

 before granting a decree of divorce on cruelty. As repeatedly emphasised

 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, cruelty must be clearly proved by the

 petitioner seeking divorce; mere accusations and counter-accusations

 do not ipso facto justify severance of the marital tie.

31. This Court, therefore, is of the clear view that the learned

 Family Court has misdirected itself in characterising the appellant’s

 conduct as cruelty. The mere fact that the wife suspected the husband’s

 association with Ajith and voiced it in various fora, on the basis of an

 admitted and unexplained proximity, cannot be treated as a reckless,

 baseless assault on his character so as to furnish a ground for

 dissolution of marriage.

32. Point (i) is, accordingly, answered in favour of the appellant-

 wife and against the respondent-husband.

33. Insofar as the desertion is concerned, the learned Family

 Court has already held that the husband has failed to prove that the

 wife deserted him from 2004 onwards. It has noted that the birth of the


 17/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 second child in 2005. The admission of the husband that, in 2006, after

 the death of the wife’s sister Jasmine, both lived together at Vaniyakudi.


 The fact that they resided together in various places, including N.G.O.

 Colony and Vaniyakudi, at least up to around 2015. These findings

 have not been challenged by the husband by way of cross appeal or

 cross objections and, in any event, they are supported by the evidence.

 Hence, this Court finds no reason to take a different view. Desertion is

 thus not established and is out of the reckoning.

34. Once the plea of cruelty fails and the plea of desertion stands

 negatived, there remains no surviving matrimonial offence proved

 against the appellant-wife within the parameters of Section 10 of the

 Indian Divorce Act, 1869. A decree of divorce is a serious matter; it

 cannot rest on conjecture, on inversion of the burden of proof or on

 misunderstanding of a spouse’s reaction to the other’s conduct.

35. It is true that the marriage between the parties has suffered

 deep strain and that they have been living separately for several years.

 However, the doctrine of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, by itself,

 is not yet a statutory ground for divorce under the Indian Divorce Act,


 18/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 1869. In the absence of any proved matrimonial offence, this Court

 cannot, in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, sustain a decree of

 dissolution merely on the ground that the marriage has broken down.

36. Point (ii) is, therefore, answered by holding that the decree of

 divorce granted by the learned Family Court cannot be sustained and is

 liable to be set aside.

37. The learned Family Court, while granting a decree of divorce,

 has recognised that the parties have two male children, Thinal and

 Jasmine Girio, born on 24.02.2004 and 26.09.2005 respectively. It

 recorded that both children are in the custody of the mother, directed

 the husband to pay a sum of Rs.10,000/- per month to each child

 towards maintenance till they complete their degree, and recognised the

 father’s visitation rights, with liberty to both parties to seek modification

 in future.

38. The present appeal is directed against the decree of divorce.

 There is no specific challenge to the custody and maintenance

 directions, and the arrangement recorded by the learned Family Court

 19/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 appears to be in consonance with the welfare of the children, who have

 all along been with the mother.

39. Even though this Court is setting aside the decree of divorce

 and dismissing the husband’s petition, the obligation of the father to

 maintain his children remains undiminished. The welfare of the

 children is paramount and independent of the vicissitudes of the

 parents’ matrimonial dispute.

40. In the facts and circumstances, this Court is of the view that

 the custody of the minor children shall continue with the appellant-

 mother. The directions issued by the learned Family Court requiring the

 respondent-father to pay Rs.10,000/- per month per child towards

 maintenance till they complete their degree, are just and proper and

 deserve to be maintained, subject to any appropriate modification that

 either party may seek in separate proceedings on proof of change in

 circumstances. The father’s visitation rights, as broadly indicated by the

 learned Family Court, shall also continue, subject to the children’s

 convenience and educational commitments, and subject further to the

 condition that such access shall not disturb their peace and stability.



 20/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021
41. Point (iii) is answered accordingly.
42. In the result, the Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is allowed.

43. The judgment and decree dated 27.03.2019 passed in I.D.O.P.

 No.86 of 2018 on the file of the learned Family Court, Kanyakumari at

 Nagercoil, in so far as it grants a decree for dissolution of marriage

 between the appellant and the respondent, are hereby set aside.

44. Consequently, I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 filed by the respondent-

 husband under Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, shall

 stand dismissed.

45. Notwithstanding the dismissal of the divorce petition, and in

 the paramount interest of the children.The custody of the two children,

 namely, Thinal and Jasmine Girio, shall continue with the appellant-

 mother. The respondent-father shall continue to pay a sum of Rs.

 10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand only) per month per child, towards their

 21/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 maintenance, as directed by the learned Family Court, from the date

 and in the manner indicated in the impugned judgment, subject to any

 modification that may be sought and granted in appropriate

 proceedings on proof of change in circumstances.

46. The respondent-father shall be entitled to visit the children

 and spend time with them at reasonable intervals, in such a manner as

 not to disturb their studies and routine, the exact modalities of which

 may be worked out by mutual consent, failing which either party may

 approach the learned Family Court for appropriate directions. The

 appellant shall not, in any manner, obstruct or prevent the respondent

 from making additional voluntary contributions for the welfare,

 education and future settlement of the children. There shall be no order

 as to costs in this appeal. Consequently, connected miscellaneous

 petition is closed.
47. In fine, this Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is allowed.

[P.V.,J.] [L.V.G.,J.]

 CORAM:

 THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE P.VELMURUGAN

 and

 THE HONOURABLE MRS.JUSTICE L.VICTORIA GOWRI

 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021
 and
 CMP(MD)No.5884 of 2021

 Mary Latha Regini ... Appellant / Respondent


 Vs.

 Maria James ... Respondent / Petitioner



 PRAYER: Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed under Section 19(1) of the
 Family Court Act, 1984, to call for the records pertaining to the fair and
 decreetal order in I.D.O.P.No.86 of 2018 passed by the learned Family
 Court, Kannyakumari at Nagercoil dated 27.03.2019 and set aside the
 same.

 For Appellant : Mr.K.P.Narayana Kumar

 For Respondent : No appearance




 1/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 JUDGMENT

[p_1] (Judgment of the Court was made by L.VICTORIA GOWRI, J.)


 This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed under Section 19 of the

 Family Courts Act, 1984, read with Section 55 of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869, to set aside the judgment and decree dated 27.03.2019 made in

 I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 on the file of the learned Family Court,

 Kanyakumari at Nagercoil, whereby the marriage between the appellant

 and the respondent solemnised on 08.05.2003 was dissolved under

 Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, on the ground of

 cruelty.

[p_3] Prologue:

[blockquote_1] 2. This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the

 judgment and decree of the learned Judge, Family Court, Kanyakumari

 at Nagercoil, in I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018, by which the respondent–

 husband’s petition under Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869, for dissolution of marriage on the ground of cruelty, came to be

 allowed and the marital tie between the parties was severed. The wife,

 who was the respondent before the learned Family Court, is the

 appellant before this Court.

[p_6] 3. The appeal raises, in essence, the recurring question as to

 when a spouse’s protest, suspicion and complaint regarding the

 conduct and association of the other spouse crosses the line and

 becomes “cruelty” in law, and equally, whether such protest, if founded

 upon some admitted factual substratum, can at all be branded as

 reckless and unfounded so as to furnish a ground for divorce.

[p_7] Case of the Husband before the learned Family Court:

[p_8] 4. The respondent-husband laid I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 under

 Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, seeking dissolution of

 his marriage with the appellant on the ground of cruelty and desertion.

 It is his case that the marriage between the parties was solemnised on

 08.05.2003 at the Church of Our Lady of Lourdes, Punnai Nagar,

 Nagercoil, according to Christian rites and customs and was duly

 registered under the Christian Marriage Act . Out of the wedlock, two

 male children, namely, Thinal (born on 24.02.2004) and Jasmine Girio

 (born on 26.09.2005) were born. Both spouses are educated and

 employed as teachers; the husband as a Selection Grade Teacher at

 Pallam and the wife as Headmistress of St. James High School,

 Vaniyakudi.

[p_9] 3/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

[p_10] 5. According to the husband, though the marriage subsisted in

 form, the appellant-wife never showed compassion, understanding, true

 love or affection. It is alleged that she persistently humiliated him, both

 at home and in public, including in the presence of neighbours,

 strangers and colleagues, by levelling wild accusations of adultery, and

 sodomy with young children, without any foundation. The husband

 would allege that these accusations were figments of imagination, for

 which she refused to correct herself despite his exhortations.

[p_11] 6. The husband further alleged that after the appellant took

 employment at Vaniyakudi, she gradually withdrew from the

 matrimonial home and ultimately left in the year 2004 along with her

 personal belongings and the minor children, ceased to discharge marital

 obligations, never cooked or cared for him, and refused to return to the

 matrimonial home, thereby causing mental cruelty and desertion. On

 these allegations, the husband approached the learned Family Court

 seeking dissolution of the marriage on the twin grounds of cruelty and

 desertion.

[p_12] 4/24

 Case of the Wife before the learned Family Court:

[p_14] 7. The appellant-wife entered contest and filed a detailed counter,

 stoutly denying the allegations and, in turn, levelling specific allegations

 of dowry demand, financial exploitation, physical cruelty and immoral

 conduct on the part of the husband. The appellant would state that at

 the time of marriage, her parents gave 65 sovereigns of gold jewellery to

 her, Rs.3,00,000/- in cash and household articles worth Rs.1,00,000/-,

 apart from a gold chain of 7½ sovereigns to the husband. She lived with

 the husband at Pallam from 2003 to 2006 and commuted daily to

 Vaniyakudi for her work.

[p_16] 8. It is her case that, in 2004, the husband took away 45

 sovereigns of her gold jewellery and pledged the same in the bank to

 discharge his earlier debts; that he continuously harassed her

 demanding additional dowry and even pledged her thali chain in 2005.

 That on 21.08.2004 he assaulted her and drove her out of the

 matrimonial home to extract more money from her parental family, and

 that she was brought back on 26.12.2004 on his assurance of good

 behaviour.

[p_17] 5/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

[p_18] 9. She further alleged that, on the husband threatening to commit

 suicide, she was constrained to borrow Rs.1,50,000/- at 36% interest

 from her colleagues, namely, Dioceis Mary, Seeli and Amalapushpam,

 and handed it over to him to clear his debts. On the demise of her sister

 Jasmine on 16.05.2006, she shifted to her parental house at

 Vaniyakudi along with her mother and, at that time, the husband also

 lived with her there. It is alleged that during this period, he sold his

 Pallam house for Rs.2,00,000/- without her knowledge and, when

 questioned, took away the minor children and disappeared, compelling

 her to approach the police for their return.

[p_20] 10. The appellant further stated that, anticipating that she would

 get regular Government salary, the husband once again sought reunion

 and they stayed in a rented house at N.G.O. Colony in 2008, and later

 returned to Vaniyakudi. She claims to have spent about Rs.2,00,000/-

 from her arrears towards clearing his debts. At his instance, she also

 obtained a loan of Rs.3,00,000/- from the Teachers’ Society, out of

 which, according to her, the husband took Rs.2,70,000/- and

 absconded, leaving her to shoulder the repayment alone.

[p_21] 11. The gravest allegation made by the wife is that the husband

 developed an undesirable association with a young man by name Ajith,

 hailing from Kootumangalam; that he used to visit a house at

 Kootumangalam frequently in 2014, return home late in the night, and

 later, in 2015, took a separate rented house at Pallam and stayed with

 the said Ajith, even admitting him in a local school showing himself as

 guardian. In this context, she claims to have lodged a complaint before

 the All Women Police Station, Colachel, wherein, according to her, the

 husband admitted that he stayed with a boy at Pallam.

[p_22] 12. The appellant would say that she placed her grievance before

 the Kootumangalam Village President and village elders; that the village

 President warned the husband and Ajith’s family; and that, in spite of

 such intervention, the husband continued his association with Ajith,

 thereby giving rise to her suspicion. She denies having deserted the

 husband, denies having humiliated him without basis and asserts that

 whatever she said and did was in response to his own conduct and

 financial and emotional abuse. She, therefore, prayed for dismissal of

 the divorce petition.

 Proceedings before the learned Family Court:

[p_25] 13. Before the learned Family Court, the husband examined

 himself as P.W.1 and produced Exs.P1 to P5. The wife examined herself

 as R.W.1 and produced Exs.R1 to R4. The learned Family Court framed

 issues, inter alia, as to (i) whether the husband had proved cruelty, (ii)

 whether he had proved desertion, and (iii) whether he was entitled to a

 decree of divorce and consequential reliefs.

[p_27] 14. Ultimately, while holding that desertion was not proved, the

 learned Family Court concluded that the wife’s allegations about the

 husband’s association with Ajith and her imputations of

 immoral/unnatural conduct, being unsubstantiated and reckless,

 amounted to mental cruelty. On that basis alone, it granted a decree for

 dissolution of marriage, while also granting custody of the children to

 the wife and directing payment of monthly maintenance to them.

[p_28] Grounds of Appeal:

[p_30] 15. Aggrieved, the wife has preferred the present appeal, raising

 the following, among other, grounds:

[p_31] 8/24

[blockquote_3] https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 The order passed by the Family Court, Kanyakumari, on

 assumptions is unknown to law and liable to be interfered with. The

 learned Trial Court failed to see that the petitioner–husband, who

 approached the Court, had the burden to prove the allegations, and

 that the burden is not on the respondent–wife. The learned Trial Court

 ought to have dismissed the petition for dissolution of marriage, as the

 same was filed by the husband to shield his own illegality and

 misconduct. A person who has committed a wrong cannot be permitted

 to benefit from his own wrong. The factum of cruelty has to be decided

 on the circumstances of each case independently and on the totality of

 evidence. The specific allegation that the husband had a relationship

 with one Ajith has, according to the appellant, been substantially

 admitted by him in his deposition. The husband’s own testimony

 reveals an unexplained and unusual attachment with Ajith and his stay

 with the said boy, which the appellant was entitled to question; her

 reaction to that cannot be termed cruelty. A spouse’s protest against the

 illegal or unnatural behaviour of the other spouse cannot be termed

 cruelty; in other words, reality cannot be branded as cruelty. The

 discussion of the learned Trial Court is self-contradictory inasmuch as,

 in paragraphs 20 and 21 of the impugned judgment, it treats the

 disputes as trivial, yet in paragraphs 27 and 28 of the impugned

 judgment, it proceeds on assumptions to hold cruelty proved. The


 9/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 learned Trial Court failed to give due weight to the admitted fact of the

 husband’s stay with Ajith, thereby erroneously treating the appellant’s

 apprehensions as reckless.

[p_32] 16. Heard the learned counsel for the appeallant and carefully

 perused the materials available on record.

[p_34] Points for Determination:

[p_36] 17. In the light of the pleadings, evidence and grounds of appeal,

 the following points arise for consideration:

[blockquote_5] (i) Whether the learned Family Court was right in holding that the

 respondent-husband had proved cruelty on the part of the appellant-

[p_38] wife within the meaning of Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act,

 1869?

[p_40] (ii) Whether the decree of divorce granted by the learned Family

 Court is sustainable in law on the evidence on record?

[p_41] (iii) What order is required to be made regarding the welfare of the

 minor children and maintenance, consequent upon the decision on

 Points (i) and (ii)?

[p_42] 10/24

 Analysis:

[p_44] 18. It is well settled that while an Appellate Court would

 ordinarily be slow to interfere with findings of fact rendered by a Court

 of first instance, where such findings are based on misapplication of

 law, non-consideration of relevant evidence, or on impermissible

 assumptions, the Appellate Court is not only empowered but duty

 bound to reappreciate the evidence, particularly in matrimonial causes

 where the consequence is civil death of the marriage and serious social

 and personal repercussions.

[p_46] 19. The learned Family Court has extracted and relied on the

 principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Shobha Rani v.

 Madhukar Reddi1 , V. Bhagat v. D. Bhagat2 , Praveen Mehta v.

 Inderjit Mehta3 , Jayachandra v. Aneel Kaur4 , and Naveen Kohli v.

 Neelu Kohli5 , as also Sirajmohmedkhan Janmohamadkhan v.


 1 (1988) 1 SCC 105


 2 (1994) 1 SCC 337


 3 (2002) 5 SCC 706


 4 (2005) 2 SCC 22


 5 (2006) 4 SCC 558

 11/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 Hafizunnisa Yasinkhan6.

[p_48] 20. There can be no quarrel with the propositions emerging

 therefrom, namely, cruelty may be physical or mental, intentional or

 unintentional. Mental cruelty is a matter of inference from cumulative

 facts and circumstances and is to be assessed in the context of the

 parties’ social status, background and milieu. Mere trivial irritations,

 quarrels and normal “wear and tear” of married life do not amount to

 cruelty. Reckless, baseless and unsubstantiated allegations which

 gravely assault the character, honour and reputation of the other

 spouse can, in an appropriate case, constitute mental cruelty. The real

 question, however, is whether, on the facts of the present case, the

 appellant’s conduct answers the test of mental cruelty as understood in

 the above decisions. It is in this area that the learned Family Court, in

 the considered opinion of this Court, has misdirected itself.

[p_49] 21. The pivot of the learned Family Court’s finding on cruelty is

 that the wife allegedly levelled baseless imputations of

 immoral/unnatural conduct and undesirable association with the

 young man Ajith and, without any foundational material, branded the

 6 AIR 1981 SC 1972

 12/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 husband as one having sexual relations with young boys. Proceeding on

 that premise, the learned Family Court held that such aspersions

 constituted grave mental cruelty.

[p_51] 22. However, a careful reading of the cross-examination of R.W.1

 (wife) and P.W.1 (husband), which has been extracted in the lower Court

 judgment, presents a more nuanced picture. R.W.1, in her cross-

 examination, has consistently deposed that the husband and the boy

 Ajith used to go together wherever they went. The husband used to visit

 a certain house at Kootumangalam frequently and return late in the

 night. The husband admitted the said Ajith in a school at Pallam as the

 guardian of that boy. She approached the village elders and the Village

 President, and the President warned the husband and Ajith’s family.

 She had been raising these issues not only at home, but also before the

 schools where they worked and before the police, from 2015 onwards.

[p_52] 23. Significantly, the husband, in his cross-examination, has not

 denied that he had admitted Ajith in school as guardian, nor has he

 given any convincing explanation for his staying with and frequent

 association with the said boy. The learned Family Court has recorded



 13/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 that none from Ajith’s family has complained and, therefore, the wife’s

 allegations are reckless. This reasoning, with respect, reverses the

 burden and overlooks the admitted factual substratum.

[p_53] 24. It is not the appellant-wife who was living with Ajith; it was

 the husband who, by his own conduct in taking a separate rented

 house, staying with the boy and functioning as his guardian, created

 circumstances which, in a conservative and closely-knit rural milieu,

 would naturally generate suspicion. Once these admitted facts stand,

 the wife’s act of questioning such association and voicing her

 apprehensions cannot be branded as entirely baseless or malicious.

[p_54] 25. The law on cruelty does not intend to punish a spouse merely

 for reacting to unusual or unexplained conduct of the other spouse.

 When one spouse places herself in circumstances that objectively

 provoke anxiety, suspicion and protest, the other spouse’s reaction

 cannot, without more, be converted into a matrimonial offence. As the

 learned counsel for the appellant rightly contended, “reality cannot be

 cruelty”; a protest grounded in a real, admitted or reasonably

 perceivable situation cannot be equated with reckless slander.



 14/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

[p_55] 26. The learned Family Court has, in paragraphs 20 and 21 of its

 judgment, itself recorded that the parties had trivial disputes and

 misunderstandings. They had periods of reunion after temporary

 separation. There is a general breakdown in marital relations, with both

 sides having grievances. At the same time, in paragraphs 27 and 28 of

 the judgment, the learned Family Court proceeds to hold that the wife’s

 allegations, being reckless, by themselves constitute cruelty. This

 internal inconsistency, pointed out in the grounds of appeal, is well-

 founded. The learned Family Court has not undertaken the required

 exercise of assessing whether, in the context of the admitted facts, the

 wife’s statements were wholly unanchored or whether they were a

 response, albeit emotionally charged and perhaps exaggerated, to the

 husband’s own inexplicable proximity to Ajith.

[p_57] 27. Further, the learned Family Court has not adverted to the

 settled principle that to constitute cruelty, the conduct must be “grave

 and weighty” and of such severity as to make it impossible for the

 wronged spouse to reasonably be expected to live with the other. The

 evidence on record, even if accepted at the highest for the husband,

 only shows that the wife repeatedly complained, questioned and

 protested, sometimes in public fora. Annoyance, embarrassment or


 15/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 wounded ego cannot, by themselves, be equated with cruelty within the

 meaning of Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869.

[p_58] 28. The husband has not produced any independent witness from

 his workplace or from the village community to show that the wife

 indulged in a sustained campaign to defame him, or that his mental

 balance and social standing were so impaired by her conduct that

 cohabitation became impossible. His case rests substantially on his own

 testimony; there is no contemporaneous material (such as complaints

 by him, counselling records reflecting her refusal to mend her ways,

 etc.) to support the plea that she crossed the legal threshold of cruelty.

[p_59] 29. On the contrary, the wife’s version of dowry-related

 harassment, financial exploitation and domestic violence finds partial

 support in the admitted facts that the husband admits to sale of the

 Pallam house and to having remained away with the children,

 compelling her to go to the police (Ex.R1). He does not specifically deny

 having taken monies from the wife or having pressurised her to obtain

 loans, though the quantum and details are not fully proved.




 16/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

[p_60] 30. In a situation where both sides level allegations and the

 evidence is a word-against-word contest, Courts must tread cautiously

 before granting a decree of divorce on cruelty. As repeatedly emphasised

 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, cruelty must be clearly proved by the

 petitioner seeking divorce; mere accusations and counter-accusations

 do not ipso facto justify severance of the marital tie.

[p_61] 31. This Court, therefore, is of the clear view that the learned

 Family Court has misdirected itself in characterising the appellant’s

 conduct as cruelty. The mere fact that the wife suspected the husband’s

 association with Ajith and voiced it in various fora, on the basis of an

 admitted and unexplained proximity, cannot be treated as a reckless,

 baseless assault on his character so as to furnish a ground for

 dissolution of marriage.

[p_63] 32. Point (i) is, accordingly, answered in favour of the appellant-

 wife and against the respondent-husband.

[p_65] 33. Insofar as the desertion is concerned, the learned Family

 Court has already held that the husband has failed to prove that the

 wife deserted him from 2004 onwards. It has noted that the birth of the


 17/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 second child in 2005. The admission of the husband that, in 2006, after

 the death of the wife’s sister Jasmine, both lived together at Vaniyakudi.


 The fact that they resided together in various places, including N.G.O.

 Colony and Vaniyakudi, at least up to around 2015. These findings

 have not been challenged by the husband by way of cross appeal or

 cross objections and, in any event, they are supported by the evidence.

 Hence, this Court finds no reason to take a different view. Desertion is

 thus not established and is out of the reckoning.

[p_67] 34. Once the plea of cruelty fails and the plea of desertion stands

 negatived, there remains no surviving matrimonial offence proved

 against the appellant-wife within the parameters of Section 10 of the

 Indian Divorce Act, 1869. A decree of divorce is a serious matter; it

 cannot rest on conjecture, on inversion of the burden of proof or on

 misunderstanding of a spouse’s reaction to the other’s conduct.

[p_68] 35. It is true that the marriage between the parties has suffered

 deep strain and that they have been living separately for several years.

 However, the doctrine of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, by itself,

 is not yet a statutory ground for divorce under the Indian Divorce Act,


 18/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 1869. In the absence of any proved matrimonial offence, this Court

 cannot, in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, sustain a decree of

 dissolution merely on the ground that the marriage has broken down.

[p_69] 36. Point (ii) is, therefore, answered by holding that the decree of

 divorce granted by the learned Family Court cannot be sustained and is

 liable to be set aside.

[p_71] 37. The learned Family Court, while granting a decree of divorce,

 has recognised that the parties have two male children, Thinal and

 Jasmine Girio, born on 24.02.2004 and 26.09.2005 respectively. It

 recorded that both children are in the custody of the mother, directed

 the husband to pay a sum of Rs.10,000/- per month to each child

 towards maintenance till they complete their degree, and recognised the

 father’s visitation rights, with liberty to both parties to seek modification

 in future.

[p_73] 38. The present appeal is directed against the decree of divorce.

 There is no specific challenge to the custody and maintenance

 directions, and the arrangement recorded by the learned Family Court

 19/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021


 appears to be in consonance with the welfare of the children, who have

 all along been with the mother.

[p_75] 39. Even though this Court is setting aside the decree of divorce

 and dismissing the husband’s petition, the obligation of the father to

 maintain his children remains undiminished. The welfare of the

 children is paramount and independent of the vicissitudes of the

 parents’ matrimonial dispute.

[p_77] 40. In the facts and circumstances, this Court is of the view that

 the custody of the minor children shall continue with the appellant-

 mother. The directions issued by the learned Family Court requiring the

 respondent-father to pay Rs.10,000/- per month per child towards

 maintenance till they complete their degree, are just and proper and

 deserve to be maintained, subject to any appropriate modification that

 either party may seek in separate proceedings on proof of change in

 circumstances. The father’s visitation rights, as broadly indicated by the

 learned Family Court, shall also continue, subject to the children’s

 convenience and educational commitments, and subject further to the

 condition that such access shall not disturb their peace and stability.



 20/24



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 12/01/2026 03:20:31 pm )
 C.M.A.(MD)No.606 of 2021

[p_78] 41. Point (iii) is answered accordingly.

[p_80] 42. In the result, the Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is allowed.

[p_81] 43. The judgment and decree dated 27.03.2019 passed in I.D.O.P.

 No.86 of 2018 on the file of the learned Family Court, Kanyakumari at

[p_82] 44. Consequently, I.D.O.P. No.86 of 2018 filed by the respondent-

 husband under Section 10(ix)(x) of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, shall

[p_84] 45. Notwithstanding the dismissal of the divorce petition, and in

 the paramount interest of the children.The custody of the two children,

 namely, Thinal and Jasmine Girio, shall continue with the appellant-

 mother. The respondent-father shall continue to pay a sum of Rs.

 10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand only) per month per child, towards their

 maintenance, as directed by the learned Family Court, from the date
